video_title: MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets
gist: CrossBorder Capital's Michael Howell tells MacroVoices the global liquidity cycle peaked at the end of 2025 and is roughly 60% through its decline — not because central banks are tightening but because strong real economies are draining money out of financial markets — with a trough unlikely before mid-to-late 2027. He is 100% convinced the Fed's next move under Kevin Warsh is a hike, sees the setup rhyming with late 2021/early 2022 (S&P -25%, Bitcoin -75%), and argues gold's cycle is driven by PBOC liquidity and China's internal yuan devaluation, with a mean-reverting gold/oil ratio implying $135-200 oil if gold holds above $4,000.

themes.theme: Where we are in the liquidity cycle

insights.claim: Howell's global liquidity cycle for advanced economies bottomed in late 2022, peaked at the end of 2025, and is now falling — with the growth rate of liquidity, not its absolute level, being what matters for asset pricing.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: Dates the regime change precisely: risk assets have been operating against a deteriorating liquidity impulse since the start of 2026, which is the frame for everything else in the episode.

insights.claim: The liquidity decline is not caused by central bank tightening but by strong real economies dragging money out of the financial sector — Howell's principle being that all money that is anywhere must be somewhere, so money in the real economy is not in markets.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: A non-obvious inversion: good economic data is bad for asset prices through the liquidity channel, independent of what the Fed does — which explains why strong ISM prints coincide with market stress.
insights.quote: all money that is anywhere must be somewhere. And um effectively if it's in the real economy, it's not in financial markets and vice versa

insights.claim: Howell puts the cycle roughly 60% through its decline and says a trough is unlikely within six months, most probably arriving in mid-to-late 2027.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: A dated horizon for the drawdown: roughly another year of deteriorating liquidity, which argues against buying a Q4 2026 bottom in liquidity-sensitive assets.

insights.claim: Liquidity leads the real economy by roughly 15-18 months, so a late-2025 liquidity peak implies the world economy keeps expanding well into 2027 and possibly early 2028, sustaining commodity demand.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: The specific lead time that makes the trade actionable: sell financial assets into a real economy that keeps running hot, and own the commodities that economy consumes.

insights.claim: The financial system now creates liquidity endogenously through collateral: roughly 80% of all lending in the world economy is collateral-based, so rising asset prices raise collateral values, which raise borrowing capacity, which raises liquidity — a self-reinforcing loop outside central bank control.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: Explains why liquidity cycles overshoot in both directions and why central banks cannot cleanly reverse them — the reflexivity runs through collateral values, not policy rates.

insights.claim: Howell's asset allocation cycle has four regimes — calm, speculation, turbulence, rebound — and places markets now in 'speculation', where returns are still available but volatility is high and return quality poor, which he says explains why many asset managers are down this year despite rising indices.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: A diagnostic for the current tape: index gains masking dispersion, which argues for selectivity and reduced beta rather than a wholesale exit.

insights.claim: The signal to move from turbulence to rebound is an inflection in the liquidity data followed almost immediately by bull steepening in yield curves, plus serious price damage in commodity markets — and Howell says we are a long way from that point.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete, monitorable checklist for the next major asset allocation shift rather than relying on price alone.

insights.claim: Howell argues every historical asset bubble has had a large liquidity expansion as its root cause — including the current 'everything bubble' and the run in Korean equities where domestic liquidity has been skyrocketing — and that after every bubble comes a bust.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: Reduces bubble-spotting to a single observable: track domestic liquidity growth, which currently flags Korea as an identifiable late-stage move.

insights.claim: Howell says his conviction that the Fed's next move is a rate hike is 100%, based on the 2-year Treasury yield being elevated and having broken above SOFR — a relationship an AI analysis of the data told him predicts policy rates correctly 85% of the time in both directions.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: A maximum-conviction call against consensus positioning for cuts — with a specific, checkable indicator (2-year versus SOFR spread) as the tell.

insights.claim: Howell's core structural claim is that central banks do not control interest rates — the market does, and the long end drives the short end rather than the textbook reverse — so a president demanding cuts cannot get them while nominal GDP growth is pushing yields up.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: If correct, political pressure on the Fed is largely irrelevant to the rate path — which means positioning for policy-driven cuts is positioning against nominal GDP.
insights.quote: central banks don't control interest rates. They may think they do. The market controls interest rates and it's the long end which drives the short end

insights.claim: Howell reads Warsh's FOMC messaging as wanting markets to do the tightening for him — letting bond yields rise while maintaining front-end liquidity through an ample-reserves regime — which is a recipe for a steepening curve even though the market wants to flatten it.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: Sets up the episode's title trade: a policy-driven steepening fighting a cycle-driven bear flattening, with the resolution determining duration positioning.

insights.claim: Howell puts US nominal GDP growth at 6-8%, driven by fiscal spending, the AI boom and deglobalization capex and inventory building — and says extrapolating the historical relationship makes a 10-year Treasury testing 6% entirely plausible.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: A specific yield target well above consensus, anchored in a nominal GDP framework that has tracked bond yields since the Treasury-Fed Accord.

insights.claim: Treasury bills are now 22% of outstanding federal debt against a stated Treasury preference of 15-20%, and Howell thinks the share could rise toward the ~30% last seen in the early 2000s — which he says would be very bad for the dollar and would make gold shoot up.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: A trackable funding metric with a direct trade attached: bill share rising above 22% is the tell for dollar weakness and gold strength.

insights.claim: Howell frames bank absorption of massive government issuance — whatever the maturity — as monetization that causes currency turmoil, with Japan as the live example: the yen sells off until the authorities finally tighten.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: Gives a mechanism linking fiscal issuance to currency depreciation that bypasses the central bank balance sheet — with the yen as the leading indicator of where the dollar could follow.

insights.claim: Japanese nominal GDP growth is above 4% while the 10-year JGB sits nearer 3%, so Howell expects JGB yields to keep climbing toward 4% as yield suppression ends and the authorities keep short rates low.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: A quantified gap between Japanese fundamentals and bond pricing — the source of continued yen weakness and a global duration risk if JGB repricing accelerates.

insights.claim: Howell's Fed tightening-cycle analysis shows the current cycle tracking the 1985-2025 average path, implying at least another six months of intensified tightening before any hint of an inflection.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: A six-month minimum horizon of monetary headwind — the timing constraint on any bullish reallocation into risk assets.

insights.claim: Howell explicitly likens the current setup to late 2021/early 2022, reminding listeners that the S&P fell 25% and Bitcoin fell 75% in that episode — with some of the crypto drawdown already in the bag this time.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: A calibrated analogue for downside magnitude — and an argument that crypto's drawdown is further along than equities'.

themes.theme: China's internal devaluation and the gold trade

insights.claim: Howell's central China thesis: Beijing must devalue debt domestically by raising internal prices and wages relative to nominal debt while holding the USD/CNY cross stable — achievable via capital controls, large FX reserves and compliant state banks — and gold is the expression of that internal devaluation.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: The single most important framework in the episode: it makes gold a China-policy trade rather than a Fed or geopolitics trade, and implies dollar gold keeps rising while the currency cross stays pinned.

insights.claim: Chinese government bond yields at 1.7% are the only major bond market where yields are falling, reflecting lackluster growth, disinflation or deflation and rising debt burdens created by years of tight liquidity defending the yuan.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: China is running the opposite cycle to the rest of the world — which makes Chinese assets a diversifier and Chinese stimulus a distinct, non-Fed catalyst for commodities.

insights.claim: Howell's daily reconstruction of the PBOC balance sheet shows liquidity taps turned off on 2 March and turned back on almost exactly the day the MOU was signed, with gold tracking both moves — which he presents as proof by association rather than inside knowledge.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: Gives a specific, high-frequency instrument to trade gold off — PBOC open market operations — and dates the current gold rally's cause precisely.

insights.claim: Howell says gold's 2022 breakaway from its historical relationship with real interest rates was not about Russia but about the PBOC turning on liquidity aggressively — a correlation he shows in both levels and weekly changes.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: If the real-rates model for gold is genuinely broken and replaced by PBOC liquidity, then most Western gold frameworks are mis-specified and will keep generating wrong signals.

insights.claim: Howell argues the yuan gold price is the correct metric because the Shanghai Gold Exchange is now the marginal pricer of gold worldwide, eclipsing COMEX and London — and yuan gold bounced exactly off its trend line at about 27,000 yuan.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: A practical change in what to watch — yuan gold and its 27,000 trend line as the level that defines the trade, not the dollar price.

insights.claim: Howell separates the two monetary hedges by driver: gold and precious metals respond to PBOC liquidity and Asian demand, while crypto responds to global and specifically Federal Reserve liquidity — which is why gold is outperforming and crypto is under a cloud.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: Resolves the puzzle of gold and Bitcoin diverging: they are not substitutes but exposures to different central banks, so both can be owned for different cycle timings.

insights.claim: Beyond China's historic debts, Howell sees Western future debts — aging demographics, defense spending and government procurement against tapped-out tax capacity — forcing progressively more debt monetization, giving gold a second, longer-run driver.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: Two independent structural bids for gold — Chinese internal devaluation now and Western monetization later — which he calls close to the top of his conviction list over the medium term.

insights.claim: After a 30% correction, Howell would not bet on new all-time highs in gold by year-end but thinks the trend is in place and it might get close — with silver outperforming gold as his confirmation signal, which he says has just started happening over a few trading days.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: A calibrated near-term view with a specific confirmation trigger — silver's relative performance — that a trader can monitor daily.

insights.claim: Howell's commodity sequencing has precious metals kicking off the cycle, followed by industrial metals, then foodstuffs, then energy at the back end — and industrial metals have clearly outperformed gold this year, putting energy next.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: A rotation map with a dated position: energy is the leg that hasn't run yet, which is where Howell says he is invested.

insights.claim: Howell's gold/oil ratio analysis shows the ratio is strongly mean-reverting with essentially no trend since 1970, and it moves with the liquidity cycle — rising as liquidity lifts gold, falling as the real economy lifts oil.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: The cleanest cross-commodity relative value framework in the episode — and it says the downswing of liquidity is structurally bullish oil versus gold.

insights.claim: Triangulating a $4,000 gold floor against the long-run gold/oil ratio of about 20x implies $200 oil, and even a more conservative 30x ratio implies $135 — numbers Howell presents as a what-if rather than a forecast.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: Even the conservative version of this arithmetic implies oil roughly 60% above spot — a substantially different distribution than consensus energy forecasts.

insights.claim: Howell explicitly rejects the consensus that oil crashes once the Hormuz crisis resolves and UAE-led OPEC supply returns, saying he thinks oil prices go up significantly and that he is heavily invested in energy stocks.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: A direct positioning statement against the supply-normalization consensus, grounded in a demand-and-currency framework rather than barrel counting.

insights.claim: Howell warns the combination is self-limiting: rising oil prices have historically been an ending feature of bull markets, so higher yields plus higher energy argues for scaling back beta in equities and risk assets.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital)
insights.so_what: Ties the commodity bull case to the equity bear case — the same forces that make energy work are what end the equity cycle.

insights.claim: Ceresna's trade of the week is a GLD bull call spread expiring 16 October 2026 — buying the $410 call for about $15 and selling the $450 call at $4.50 for a net $10.50 debit on a $40-wide spread, roughly 3:1 payoff — using gold's steep right-tail skew to subsidize the long call.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: A defined-risk expression of Howell's gold view that explicitly monetizes the expensive upside skew rather than paying for it outright.

insights.claim: COT positioning as of 4 August shows an extreme divergence within equities: S&P speculators at the 96th percentile and the Dow at the 99th on a one-year basis, while Nasdaq positioning sits near zero after 25,000 fresh shorts took the net position to 35,000 contracts short.
insights.speaker: Macrovoices market desk
insights.so_what: New shorts rather than long liquidation in the Nasdaq — likely paired against overextended semiconductor and Mag 7 exposure — sets up a squeeze if tech re-participates.

insights.claim: The desk notes the S&P has held fresh all-time highs rather than mean-reverting, sees 8,000 possible within weeks on a catalyst, and estimates it would take roughly a 400-point decline to cause technical damage that triggers systematic selling — meaning a 200-point pullback gets bought.
insights.speaker: Macrovoices market desk
insights.so_what: Quantifies the buffer before trend-following flows turn — a useful risk threshold for anyone fading the rally.

insights.claim: The Japanese yen intervention drove USD/JPY from a 164 handle to 155 and forced a 118,000-contract weekly swing to the long side — 25% of open interest, the largest weekly change across all markets — yet yen positioning remains net short, leaving more short covering possible.
insights.speaker: Macrovoices market desk
insights.so_what: A quarter of yen traders were forced out in one week and the position is still short — the fuel for another violent move if intervention or BOJ tightening recurs.

insights.claim: September Fed hike odds have fallen from better than 50/50 to roughly a two-thirds probability of no move, and with only three meetings left and the October meeting falling within a week of the election, the desk thinks a hike may be pushed to December or not happen at all.
insights.speaker: Macrovoices market desk
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts Howell's 100% hike conviction — the market is pricing the opposite, which is precisely what makes his call a trade rather than a consensus view.

insights.claim: Bond positioning is bifurcated: the 2-year sits at the 100th percentile of its one-year range on heavy short covering while the 10-year is at the zeroth percentile, with the 30-year yield near 5.25% and shorts still pressing the long end.
insights.speaker: Macrovoices market desk
insights.so_what: Positioning is set up for exactly the steepening Howell attributes to Warsh's policy mix — front end covered, long end short.

insights.claim: Uranium futures flatlined between $85 and $87 for three months before upticking, with the URA uranium producer basket rallying almost 25% trough to peak over two weeks and reclaiming its 50-day moving average.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Equities leading the commodity is the classic early signal of an accumulation cycle — worth watching as the next leg of the broader commodity rotation.

insights.claim: Wheat speculators went from flat to 15,000 contracts net short in a week — 11,000 of them fresh shorts — and did so before reported attacks on major Russian grain infrastructure, with Russia controlling 22% of global wheat exports and similar patterns forming in soybeans and corn.
insights.speaker: Macrovoices market desk
insights.so_what: Fresh shorts positioned directly against a rising physical supply risk — the setup for a forced short-covering rally comparable to the run-up to 2022.

insights.claim: Crude has consolidated around its 50-day moving average with the desk seeing fair value elevated in the $80+ area, a plausible path back to $90 on headlines, and little chance of returning to the June low near $65 while Hormuz remains unresolved.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: A tactical floor under oil that is consistent with, though far less aggressive than, Howell's $135-200 structural triangulation.

insights.claim: Gold's roughly 10% breakout is its first sustained period above the 50-day moving average since late April's bounce, with gold speculative positioning back to neutral but silver near the zeroth percentile of its one-year range.
insights.speaker: Macrovoices market desk
insights.so_what: Silver at the zeroth percentile is the asymmetric expression of Howell's precious metals view — maximum room for positioning to rebuild if the turn is real.
